title: Automating postmarketing pharmacovigilance with large language model agents
authors: Zhang, R.; Zhou, Y.; Chui, C. S. L.; Yu, D.; Wu, Z.; Luo, R.
abstract: Postmarketing pharmacovigilance relies on spontaneous adverse event reporting and labor-intensive observational studies, which suffer from underreporting and delayed risk detection. Large language model (LLM) agents could automate real-world evidence generation, but generalist agents make ad hoc analytical decisions that compromise epidemiological validity and reproducibility. Here we present MedCheckpoint, a multi-agent LLM system for automated postmarketing pharmacovigilance. MedCheckpoint grounds each analytical stage in a curated, source-traceable medical knowledge base, locks core study-design parameters before execution, performs patient-level analyses with human-written deterministic statistical tools, and enforces checkpoint rules that abort infeasible analyses, with optional human-in-the-loop review. We evaluated MedCheckpoint using a 54-question benchmark on a dual-purpose simulated electronic health record (EHR) testbed of 2.7 million individuals, designed with reliable clinical signals to evaluate routine analytical accuracy alongside spurious signals to stress-test system rigor. Across the benchmark, MedCheckpoint outperformed two coding-agent baselines in report quality across five dimensions rated by three independent LLM judges (overall means 4.81-4.88 versus 4.25-4.55 and 4.02-4.29) and yielded higher run-to-run consistency (mean within-question standard deviation 0.116-0.186 versus up to 0.440). Crucially, while baselines failed on up to 2 of 21 runs when handling infeasible comparisons or unmeasurable outcomes, MedCheckpoint produced no misleading failures across all seven stress-test trap questions with known data limitations. MedCheckpoint enables reliable, auditable, and scalable pharmacovigilance analysis.

infographic.key_insight: MedCheckpoint combines LLM agents with fixed study designs, deterministic statistical tools, and feasibility checkpoints to improve automated drug-safety research reliability.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The system could support more auditable postmarketing drug-safety analyses, but its performance in real clinical datasets remains unproven.
method: Ground analytical stages in curated, source-traceable medical knowledge.
Lock core study-design parameters and use human-written deterministic tools for patient-level analyses.
Abort infeasible analyses through checkpoints, with optional human review.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 54 questions using simulated EHRs for 2.7 million individuals, MedCheckpoint outperformed two coding-agent baselines on LLM-rated report quality and consistency, with no misleading failures across seven stress-test trap questions.
infographic.watch_item: Simulated data and LLM-judged report quality do not establish real-world drug-safety detection performance.
infographic.paper_title: Automating postmarketing pharmacovigilance with large language model agents

title: Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST): Comparing Self-Triage Systems and Multiple Generations of OpenAI Models Against Preliminary Expert Consensus
authors: Kroll, L. E.; Seidel, A.; Schuster, J.; Steiger, E.; Schoepke, T.; von Stillfried, D.; BeST Study Group,
abstract: As digital self-triage becomes more widely used, quality assurance requires evaluation of both emergency recognition and overall agreement with clinical judgement, including how these outcomes differ across generations of large language models. The Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST) project intends to provide a framework to compare systems for digital self-triage against a medical gold standard in Germany. As a first step in developing and demonstrating the methodology, we compared study-specific implementations of SmED 5.4.11 accessed via API and Infermedica Engine API via Microsoft Azure Healthcare Agent Service with five structured OpenAI configurations spanning multiple model generations: gpt-4.1, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-sol, and gpt-6-astra. The manufacturers of SmED and Infermedica offer MDR-certified Class IIb triage products, but these certified products were not directly evaluated. An LLM-based patient actor covered 480 physician-curated vignettes derived from German routine triage data. A pool of seven physicians provided preliminary reference classifications and consensus for 480 vignettes. Recommendations were mapped to three urgency categories-emergency, acute, and not urgent-and evaluated using winsorised weights derived from routine triage frequencies. Weighted emergency sensitivity ranged from 51.3% (95% CI 35.566.3%) for gpt-4.1 to 99.9% (99.7-100.0%) for gpt-6-astra. Weighted exact three-category agreement (accuracy) ranged from 54.4% to 68.8%; gpt-4.1 achieved the highest agreement despite the lowest emergency sensitivity. No system performed best across all urgency categories. The later-generation OpenAI configurations showed a more precautionary triage profile resembling SmED, with higher sensitivity for emergency cases; gpt-6-astra showed the strongest shift. This cross-sectional comparison across model generations suggests a shift towards more precautionary triage behaviour, without establishing a longitudinal improvement in accuracy. These findings highlight the limitations of overall agreement for evaluating self-triage and support category-specific assessment. Broader expert consensus and evaluation, as well as further steps to reduce dependence on SmED-derived source data, are needed and planned before drawing conclusions about clinical safety.

infographic.key_insight: Later-generation OpenAI configurations showed higher emergency sensitivity, but no system performed best across all urgency categories.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Self-triage evaluation should assess emergency recognition separately from overall agreement, since the highest-agreement model had the lowest emergency sensitivity.
method: Compared study-specific SmED and Infermedica implementations with five structured OpenAI configurations.
Used an LLM patient actor across 480 physician-curated vignettes derived from German routine triage data.
Compared three-category urgency recommendations against preliminary physician consensus using routine-frequency-derived weights.
infographic.evidence_signal: Weighted emergency sensitivity ranged from 51.3% to 99.9%, while weighted exact three-category agreement ranged from 54.4% to 68.8%.
infographic.watch_item: Preliminary consensus and study-specific implementations limit generalizability; the comparison does not establish longitudinal accuracy improvement or evaluate the manufacturers’ certified products directly.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST): Comparing Self-Triage Systems and Multiple Generations of OpenAI Models Against Preliminary Expert Consensus

title: Generative AI Versus Primary Care Physicians from Plan Initiation to Long-Term Maintenance of Chronic Disease Self-Management: A Vignette-Based Validation Study
authors: Zhao, Z.; Yang, H.; Wang, Q.; Wang, Y.; Cheng, W.; Ma, X.
abstract: BackgroundGenerative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may provide personalised and dynamically adjustable support for chronic disease self-management. However, previous studies have largely focused on isolated questions and a limited range of evaluation dimensions. ObjectiveTo compare the quality of self-management advice generated by GenAI and primary care physicians (PCPs) across multiple stages of chronic disease management and evaluation dimensions. MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional, source-blinded comparative evaluation using 15 standardised vignettes of diabetes and hypertension derived from authentic primary care follow-up records. Each vignette comprised three sequential management stages, with medical accuracy, readability, and behaviour-change potential assessed across the three simulated stages; individualisation and multidisciplinary integration at plan initiation; contextual adaptability during acute adjustment; and empathy during long-term maintenance. The GenAI system and 22 PCPs independently generated advice which was independently rated by three clinicians, one each from general practice, endocrinology, and cardiology. across seven dimensions. Linear mixed-effects models were used for the primary comparisons, and case-level paired and physician-distribution analyses were conducted as robustness analyses. ResultsThe GenAI system achieved estimated marginal means above 4.0 in all dimensions except readability. It scored significantly higher than PCPs in six of the seven dimensions, with adjusted mean differences ranging from 1.16 to 1.56 points (P<.001). Readability was the only exception, with no significant difference between GenAI and PCPs (-0.22, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.11; P=.19). The GenAI mean exceeded the individual means of all recruited PCPs in the six dimensions but ranked at approximately the 23rd percentile for readability. ConclusionsOur findings indicated the GenAI system may generate more highly rated self-management advice than PCPs across most evaluated dimensions but offered no advantage in readability. These findings provide pre-implementation evidence for GenAI as a potential source of structured and adaptive chronic disease self-management support. Patient-level pilot studies and subsequent randomised trials are needed to determine its acceptability and effects on behaviour and clinical outcomes.

infographic.key_insight: GenAI advice scored higher than primary care physicians’ advice in six of seven evaluated dimensions, but not readability.
infographic.clinical_relevance: GenAI may support structured chronic disease self-management advice, but this study does not establish benefits for patients in clinical practice.
method: Source-blinded comparison using 15 diabetes and hypertension vignettes across three simulated management stages.
One GenAI system and 22 primary care physicians independently generated advice.
Three clinician raters assessed seven dimensions; comparisons used linear mixed-effects models and robustness analyses.
infographic.evidence_signal: GenAI’s adjusted score advantage was 1.16–1.56 points across six dimensions (P<.001), while readability showed no significant difference (−0.22; 95% CI −0.54 to 0.11).
infographic.watch_item: Vignette-based clinician ratings of one GenAI system do not establish real-world safety, patient understanding, or long-term outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Generative AI Versus Primary Care Physicians from Plan Initiation to Long-Term Maintenance of Chronic Disease Self-Management: A Vignette-Based Validation Study

title: AToP: An Explainability Framework for Transformer-Based EHR Predictions Using Attribution-Guided Temporal Pattern Mining
abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and evaluate AToP (Attribution to Temporal Patterns), a post-hoc explainability framework that converts per-token Integrated Gradients (IG) from a Transformer into structured temporal pattern narratives. Materials and MethodsAToP was applied to a single-stream Transformer trained on MIMIC-IV v3.1 (218,196 patients; 12.6% unplanned 30-day readmission). It mines frequent episodes from salient-token subsequences in the training cohort, aggregates attribution among patients whose records contain each token or pattern, and collapses near-duplicates by patient overlap. Validation used masking, reversed-order analysis, token-level faithfulness tests, and KernelSHAP comparison. ResultsThe Transformer achieved AUROC 0.77 and PR-AUC 0.34. Population-weighted attribution emphasized high-prevalence codes with small per-patient impact. Carrier-conditional attribution, the mean among patients with the token, surfaced rare high-attribution psychiatric markers including psychosis, self-harm overdose, suicidal ideation (SI), and severe major depressive disorder (MDD). Pattern-level attribution identified within-visit co-occurrences and cross-visit trajectories not captured by token rankings. Risk-increasing patterns included psychiatric sequences ({MDD, SI} [->] SI) and oncologic progressions (cancer anemia [->] ascites). Obstetric and chest pain evaluation patterns were associated with lower predicted readmission. DiscussionThe framework provides two complementary views of model predictions: carrier-conditional aggregation highlights rare, highly attributed clinical features, while temporal pattern analysis identifies within-visit combinations and cross-visit trajectories missed by token-level rankings. Masking and visit-order reversal provided evidence of correspondence with model behavior, but pattern attributions do not represent unique effects or establish clinical validity. ConclusionAToP turns a Transformers attributions into visit-anchored temporal pattern narratives, showing which events, in which order, contribute to its readmission predictions.

infographic.key_insight: AToP converts Transformer attributions into visit-anchored temporal patterns, revealing event combinations and sequences missed by token rankings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework may help researchers interpret EHR-based readmission predictions by showing which recorded events, in which order, contribute to model outputs.
method: Compute per-token Integrated Gradients for a Transformer predicting unplanned 30-day readmission.
Mine frequent temporal patterns from salient-token sequences and collapse near-duplicates by patient overlap.
Compare population-weighted and carrier-conditional attribution to distinguish common signals from rare, highly attributed features.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MIMIC-IV v3.1 data from 218,196 patients, the Transformer achieved AUROC 0.77 and PR-AUC 0.34; explanations were evaluated using masking, visit-order reversal, token-level faithfulness tests, and KernelSHAP comparison.
infographic.watch_item: Pattern attributions reflect model behavior, not unique causal effects or established clinical validity.
infographic.paper_title: AToP: An Explainability Framework for Transformer-Based EHR Predictions Using Attribution-Guided Temporal Pattern Mining

title: Silent Drift and Site-level Variance in Clinical AI: Real-world performance and subgroup analysis for post-market monitoring of an FDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for high-risk use case of pulmonary embolism
authors: Dayma, K.; Newton, C.; Kawzowicz, M.; Patel, P.; Curl, R.; Ogden, K.
abstract: BackgroundFDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for pulmonary embolism (PE) detection has been widely used; however, its performance has not been analyzed for subgroups, clinical sites, and temporal stability. MethodsThis retrospective, six-site health system study evaluated the Aidoc BriefCase PE triage model (K190072) across 14,736 CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) examinations between July 2023 and March 2026. Reference-standard PE characteristic labels were extracted from radiology reports using a zero-shot LLM pipeline validated against a radiologist-annotated 600 reports ({kappa} =0.98). Model performance was evaluated across demographics, embolus characteristics, and site. Temporal behavior was evaluated on operating point by logistic regression, with and without site adjustment, and by segmented regression. ResultsPE was present in 1,402/14,736 examinations (9.5%). Overall sensitivity was 64.1% (95% CI, 61.5-66.6%), specificity 98.8% (95% CI, 98.6-99.0%), compared with 93% sensitivity and 93.7% specificity in the FDA 510(k) summary. Sensitivity fell with peripherality (central 88.6%, lobar or segmental 63.1%, subsegmental 33.3%) and with chronicity (acute 65.5%, chronic 57.4%). Sensitivity differed significantly between the two highest-volume sites, 68.7% and 55.7% (P < .001), with CT scanner as the only variable different between the two sites. The false-positive rate fell 40% per year (P<.001) at a similar rate at two sites, while sensitivity fell 15% per year at site A (P<.036), from 72.5% to 65.0% between two halves of the study period. The manufacturer did not report model updates or threshold changes during the study period. ConclusionsDeployed sensitivity was substantially below the cleared benchmark and varied 13 points by site. The gradual shift in high specificity at the cost of low sensitivity, either from data drift or threshold change, either not monitored or not documented by the manufacturer, highlights the importance of independent continuous post-market monitoring.

infographic.key_insight: Real-world sensitivity of an FDA-cleared pulmonary embolism AI triage tool was 64.1%, versus 93% in its clearance summary, and varied by site, embolus location, and time.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Lower detection of peripheral and chronic emboli highlights why aggregate performance may obscure clinically relevant gaps in deployed AI triage.
method: Retrospective evaluation of 14,736 CT pulmonary angiography examinations across six sites, July 2023–March 2026.
Report-derived reference labels used an LLM pipeline validated against 600 radiologist-annotated reports (κ = 0.98).
Assessed subgroup and site performance, plus temporal trends using logistic and segmented regression.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 1,402 PE-positive examinations, sensitivity was 64.1% (95% CI, 61.5–66.6%) and specificity was 98.8% (98.6–99.0%); sensitivity differed by 13 percentage points between the two highest-volume sites.
infographic.watch_item: This retrospective, single-health-system study cannot establish whether temporal changes reflected data drift or undocumented model or threshold changes; independent monitoring remains important.
infographic.paper_title: Silent Drift and Site-level Variance in Clinical AI: Real-world performance and subgroup analysis for post-market monitoring of an FDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) triage tool for high-risk use case of pulmonary embolism

title: Cytokine Signatures of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Myocarditis and the Modifying Role of Clonal Hematopoiesis: A Machine-Learning and Multi-Omics Study
authors: Manchanda, N.; Chehayeb, R. J.; Hong, D.; Jeyashanmugaraja, A.; Singh, J.; Cross, J. L.; Vijayram, A.; Martinez, C. M.; Jayakrishnan, R.; Christofides, A.; Lin, D.; Im, Y.; VanOudenhove, J.; Biancon, G.; Ibrahim, E.; Ardasheva, A.; Lin, E. Y. S.; Levine, R.; Cheng, E.; Halene, S.; Hwa, J.; Smith, N.; Villani, C.; Zhu, H.; Jha, A.; Kwan, J. M.
abstract: BackgroundImmune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) myocarditis affects up to 2% of patients on ICI and has up to a 50% mortality. Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) is a risk factor for ICI myocarditis. ObjectivesTo leverage a multi-omics approach to evaluate cytokines associated with ICI myocarditis, immunosuppression resistance, CHIP in ICI myocarditis and implicated pathways and cell type contributions. Methods236 cardio-oncology patients were enrolled, including 88 who were on ICI. Cytokine profiling from patients on ICI were sampled and analyzed using machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence. Single-cell multi-omics of peripheral blood from Yale (n=19), Stanford (n=25), and MGH (n=63) evaluated cell-type contributions of cytokines and implicated pathways. Validation of Yale proteomic analyses was done using the Stanford CYTOF dataset. ResultsTop features associated with ICI myocarditis included IL13, CXCL10, PDGF-A, CCL13, CCL17 and KITlg. Top KEGG pathways associated with ICI myocarditis and immunosuppression resistant ICI myocarditis included JAK-STAT signaling, IL17 signaling and lipid/atherosclerosis pathways. At the single-cell level, the consensus signals distinguishing myocarditis from non-myocarditis across cohorts was predominantly driven by module-level JAK-STAT, T-cell, and Toll-like receptor activation. Similar transcription gene programs were activated in CHIP carriers including modules implicated in the pro-inflammatory immune response, such as NF-kappa B, IL17, MAPK, and TNF pathways within CHIP cells spanning lymphoid (cytotoxic CD8+ NKT, and natural killer cells) and myeloid lineages. ConclusionsAcross cohorts, JAK-STAT signaling emerges as a convergent and potentially actionable axis in ICI myocarditis that is further amplified in CHIP carriers, supporting cytokine-guided risk stratification and JAK-STAT-directed immunosuppression as testable strategies.

infographic.key_insight: Machine learning and multi-omics identified cytokine signatures associated with ICI myocarditis, with JAK–STAT signaling emerging across cohorts and amplified in CHIP carriers.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings suggest research targets for cytokine-guided risk stratification and pathway-directed treatment, but do not establish clinical utility or treatment benefit.
method: Machine learning and explainable AI analyzed cytokine profiles from patients receiving ICIs.
Single-cell multi-omics mapped implicated pathways and immune-cell contributions across three cohorts.
Stanford CyTOF data were used to validate Yale proteomic analyses.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study enrolled 236 cardio-oncology patients, including 88 receiving ICIs, and evaluated single-cell data from Yale (n=19), Stanford (n=25), and MGH (n=63).
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports associations but no predictive performance metrics or prospective evidence that cytokine-guided care improves outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Cytokine Signatures of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Myocarditis and the Modifying Role of Clonal Hematopoiesis: A Machine-Learning and Multi-Omics Study

title: Primary Care Quality and Inappropriate Community Antibiotic Use: Evidence from Linked Provider and Household Data
authors: Chen, Y.; Yi, H.; Rao, S.; Weber, A.; Hassmiller-Lich, K.; Sylvia, S.
abstract: Inappropriate antibiotic use presents a major global health challenge, particularly in resource-limited settings where access to quality care remains limited while access to antibiotics is relatively unrestricted. This study estimates the relationship between frontline primary care quality and community antibiotic use, drawing on detailed data from approximately 100 rural villages in China that link objective measures of village doctors clinical practice quality, assessed through unannounced standardized patient visits, to household-level antibiotic use data measured within the same communities. To mitigate potential endogeneity concerns, we employed an instrumental variable (IV) approach integrated within a double/debiased machine learning (DML) framework, using ensemble machine learning to combine information across multiple individually weak but jointly informative provider-level instruments. Higher clinical practice quality was associated with lower probabilities of inappropriate antibiotic receipt during healthcare encounters for cold or diarrhea symptoms (OLS: 6.2 percentage points; DML-IV: 9.6 percentage points) and households storing antibiotics at home for future use (OLS: 4.1 percentage points; DML-IV: 10.9 percentage points). These findings highlight the potential role of improving frontline primary care quality in community antibiotic stewardship. Methodologically, this study illustrates how causal machine learning can complement conventional econometric methods by addressing high-dimensional estimation challenges in global health economics research.

infographic.key_insight: Higher frontline primary care quality was associated with less inappropriate antibiotic receipt and less household antibiotic storage in rural China.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Improving primary care quality may support community antibiotic stewardship alongside efforts to address unrestricted antibiotic access.
method: Linked standardized-patient assessments of village doctors to household antibiotic-use data.
Compared ordinary least squares estimates with instrumental-variable double/debiased machine learning estimates.
Used ensemble machine learning to combine multiple provider-level instruments.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across approximately 100 rural villages, reported reductions were 6.2 percentage points (OLS) and 9.6 (DML-IV) for inappropriate antibiotic receipt, and 4.1 (OLS) and 10.9 (DML-IV) for household storage.
infographic.watch_item: Causal interpretation depends on instrumental-variable assumptions, and findings may not generalize beyond rural Chinese communities.
infographic.paper_title: Primary Care Quality and Inappropriate Community Antibiotic Use: Evidence from Linked Provider and Household Data

title: Use of AI-Related CPT Codes by Patient, Geographic, and Payer Characteristics in the U.S., 2021-2026
authors: Kim, E. J.; Chang, S.; Feng, J.; Bedmutha, P. S.; Poursoltan, L.; Cao, J.; Wellsjo, A.; Floyd, E.; Luo, D.; Zhu, K.; Boussina, A. J.; Holland, J.; Sitapati, A.; Hallaj, S.; Nemati, S.; Gabriel, R.; Khalessi, A.; Longhurst, C.; Singh, K.; Ramsis, M.
abstract: ImportancePayment policy for clinical artificial intelligence (AI) is changing quickly, yet national data on which AI-enabled services are used, and for whom, are limited. ObjectiveTo describe national trends in the use of AI-related Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes and how use differs by patient, geographic, and payer characteristics. Design, Setting, and ParticipantsThis serial cross-sectional study used Epic Cosmos, a deidentified electronic health record dataset, to examine 11,605,867,309 encounters among 233,628,292 US patients from January 1, 2021, to April 14, 2026. Exposures: Calendar year, age, sex, race, ethnicity, rurality, area-level social vulnerability, census region, and primary payer. Main Outcomes and MeasuresEncounters with any of 65 CPT codes that require AI, identified by matching the CPT code set to US Food and Drug Administration-listed AI-enabled devices and classified as assistive, augmentative, or autonomous using the CPT Appendix S taxonomy. ResultsOf 11.6 billion encounters, 335,349 (2.9 per 100,000) included an AI-required CPT code. The odds of an encounter with an AI-required code were 9.88 (95% CI, 9.71-10.06) times higher in 2025 than in 2021. In unadjusted comparisons, use was higher among patients aged 65 to 85 years and among those with Medicare (OR, 5.11) or Medicare Advantage (OR, 5.12) vs commercial insurance. Use was lower among Black (OR, 0.72) and Hispanic or Latino (OR, 0.34) patients, Medicaid enrollees (OR, 0.65), residents of the most socially vulnerable areas (OR, 0.53), and residents of the most rural areas (OR, 0.86). Use of automated diabetic retinopathy screening increased after the service was added to a HEDIS quality measure. One newer code (quantitative brain MRI) appeared in rural areas within months of becoming effective, whereas older codes such as retinopathy screening took years. Conclusions and RelevanceIn this cross-sectional study, billed use of AI-enabled services remained rare but grew substantially and was concentrated among older and Medicare-insured patients, with lower use among Medicaid enrollees and residents of socially vulnerable areas. As the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services restructures payment for software and launches outcome-based models, tracking who receives AI-enabled care across payment pathways will be important for equitable access. KEY POINTSO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSHow has billed use of artificial intelligence (AI)-related CPT codes changed nationally since 2021, and how does use differ by patient, geographic, and payer characteristics? FindingsIn this cross-sectional study of 11.6 billion US encounters, 2.9 per 100,000 included an AI-required CPT code. Odds of use were nearly 10 times higher in 2025 than in 2021, higher among Medicare beneficiaries, and lower among Medicaid enrollees and residents of socially vulnerable areas. MeaningBilled AI use remains rare and uneven across payers and communities, so payment policy for AI may need to be paired with monitoring of who receives AI-enabled care.

infographic.key_insight: AI-required CPT codes remained rare but had 9.88 times higher odds of appearing in encounters in 2025 than in 2021, with uneven use across patient groups.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Billed AI-enabled services were more common among older and Medicare-insured patients and less common among Medicaid enrollees and residents of socially vulnerable areas.
method: Serial cross-sectional analysis of Epic Cosmos encounters from January 2021 to April 2026.
Identified 65 AI-required CPT codes by matching CPT codes to FDA-listed AI-enabled devices.
Compared use across patient, geographic, and payer characteristics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 11.6 billion encounters involving 233.6 million US patients, 335,349 encounters included an AI-required code—2.9 per 100,000 encounters.
infographic.watch_item: CPT-coded encounters do not capture all clinical AI use, and unadjusted group differences do not establish causes of unequal use.
infographic.paper_title: Use of AI-Related CPT Codes by Patient, Geographic, and Payer Characteristics in the U.S., 2021-2026

title: Expert-level localization of fine-grained cardiac structures across the transthoracic echocardiogram
authors: Mahmoudi, E. m.; Pecco, N.; Sheashaa, H.; Baba Ali, N.; Awad, K.; Abdelfattah, F. E.; Attaripour Esfahani, S.; Scalia, I. G.; Farina, J.; Ayoub, C.; Arsanjani, R.; Grogan, M.; Kane, G.; Oh, J. K.; Banerjee, I.; Erickson, B. J.; Chao, C.-J.
abstract: Artificial intelligence models for echocardiography interpret studies without identifying the structures that support their outputs. We show that this spatial grounding does not emerge from the pretraining of current vision-language models. General-purpose and medical vision-language models and an open-vocabulary detector recalled 3% or fewer of cardiac structures and scored below a box that never sees the image. EchoLens, a detector trained on 5,912 expert-annotated structures and 4,219 Doppler signals from 136 patients, recalled 87% and localized structures as reliably as a blinded expert reader (box centre within the reference in 95.7% and 95.3% of cases). It covers 21 structures across 11 transthoracic views and 11 spectral Doppler signal types. In external data, two physicians judged 81-92% of its detections correct across all 11 views, and it identified the Doppler signal type in 83% of frames. EchoLens provides the spatial layer that grounded echocardiographic interpretation requires.

infographic.key_insight: EchoLens localized fine-grained cardiac structures at expert-comparable reliability, while tested general-purpose and medical vision-language models and an open-vocabulary detector recalled 3% or fewer.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Explicit structure localization could help ground echocardiography AI outputs in visible anatomy, though clinical benefit remains unproven.
method: Trained a detector on 5,912 expert-annotated structures and 4,219 Doppler signals from 136 patients.
Covered 21 cardiac structures across 11 transthoracic views and 11 spectral Doppler signal types.
Evaluated against a blinded expert reader and physician review of external data.
infographic.evidence_signal: EchoLens recalled 87% of structures; box centers fell within reference regions in 95.7% of cases versus 95.3% for an expert, while external review judged 81–92% of detections correct and Doppler type identification reached 83%.
infographic.watch_item: The modest training cohort and localization-focused evaluation leave broader generalizability and downstream clinical impact to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Expert-level localization of fine-grained cardiac structures across the transthoracic echocardiogram

title: Prediction of Subsolid Pulmonary Nodule Evolution from Baseline CT Using Temporal Imaging Models
authors: Bondarenko, M.; Qi, K.; Nowroozi, A.; Kim, J.; Kunzang, B.; Lee, A.; Liu, J.; Tran, N.; Weng, S.; Vella, M.; Chaudhari, G.; Schnizler, T.; Innanje, A.; Chen, T.; Sohn, J. H.
abstract: BackgroundPrediction of subsolid pulmonary nodule (SSN) progression from baseline CT may improve risk stratification and surveillance planning, but prior approaches have largely relied on fixed follow-up intervals. MethodsThis retrospective single-center study evaluated interval-aware temporal imaging models for predicting future SSN growth and morphology across heterogeneous surveillance durations. A total of 24,946 longitudinal scan pairings derived from 2,543 clinician-reviewed SSNs in 426 patients were analyzed. A discriminative deep learning model predicted interval growth from baseline CT, segmentation masks, and interscan interval information, while a temporally conditioned generative model predicted future lesion morphology. ResultsThe discriminative model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.772 (95% confidence interval: 0.704-0.818), with sensitivity of 80.2% and specificity of 58.7% on the test cohort. The generative model predicted future lesion morphology with a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.706 {+/-} 0.186. Prediction performance decreased with increasing follow-up duration, although both models generalized across intervals ranging from months to years. ConclusionInterval-aware temporal imaging models enable the prediction of future SSN growth and morphology from baseline CT while accounting for variable surveillance intervals. These findings suggest a framework for time-aware, personalized risk assessment that may support individualized surveillance strategies and future AI-assisted management of pulmonary adenocarcinoma spectrum lesions.

infographic.key_insight: Interval-aware AI models predicted subsolid pulmonary nodule growth and future morphology from baseline CT across follow-up periods ranging from months to years.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Time-aware predictions may support individualized nodule surveillance, but clinical benefit remains to be established.
method: Retrospective, single-center study of longitudinal CT scans.
Discriminative model used baseline CT, segmentation masks, and interscan intervals to predict growth.
Temporally conditioned generative model predicted future lesion morphology.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 24,946 scan pairings from 2,543 nodules in 426 patients, test growth prediction achieved an AUROC of 0.772 (95% CI: 0.704–0.818), 80.2% sensitivity, and 58.7% specificity; morphology prediction achieved Dice 0.706 ± 0.186.
infographic.watch_item: Performance declined at longer follow-up intervals, and the single-center retrospective findings require external validation before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Prediction of Subsolid Pulmonary Nodule Evolution from Baseline CT Using Temporal Imaging Models

title: Spatiotemporal mapping of ex vivo myometrial contractions in adenomyosis
authors: Huon, E.; Zig, L.; Seguard, O.; Plancke, M.; Abo, C.; Lamau, M.-C.; Dietrich, G.; Abrahami, Y.; Kouby, J.; Adam, J.; Chevalier, N. R.
abstract: ObjectiveUterine dyscontractility plays a major role in pain sensation, infertility, and adenomyosis pathogenesis. In vivo, contractility occurs in the inner myometrium and junctional zone, which is thickened in adenomyosis. We examined whether the junctional zone presents particular contractile features ex vivo by measuring contractility and oxytocin response in full-thickness serosa-to-endometrium myometrial slices retrieved from control and adenomyosis patients. DesignProspective ex vivo case-control study. SubjectsPremenopausal women following hysterectomy: adenomyosis (n = 16) and controls (n = 12). Contractility: 57 strips (11 vs 8 patients), immunofluorescence: 10 vs 9 patients. Main Outcome MeasuresWe resorted to spatiotemporal mapping, time-lapse video-based techniques used in the field of gastroenterology. We measured contraction frequency, amplitude, duration, velocity, site of origin, and propagation direction along the serosa-to-endometrium axis, before and after oxytocin. We measured oxytocin receptor density along the serosa-to-endometrium axis by immunofluorescence and machine learning-assisted segmentation. ResultsEx vivo contractile waves propagated throughout the outer and inner myometrium, with similar amplitude and frequency. Contraction frequency, amplitude, duration, and velocity did not differ between control and adenomyosis uteri. Oxytocin increased contraction frequency and velocity and systematically caused contractile waves to originate at the inner myometrium in both groups. In both groups, oxytocin receptor density was highest in the inner myometrium. Adenomyosis patients had a 1.8-fold higher oxytocin receptor density, but a smaller oxytocin-induced increase in contraction frequency. ConclusionWe provide the first ex vivo spatiotemporal time-lapse analysis of myometrial contractions. The whole myometrium contracts ex vivo, not just the inner part (junctional zone). This uniform myogenic motility is presumably inhibited neurally in vivo in the outer myometrium. Ex vivo adenomyosis basal contractility was similar to that of controls. Adenomyotic myometrium overexpressed oxytocin receptors compared to controls, but this did not translate into a stronger contractile response to oxytocin. In both groups, oxytocin caused contractile waves to originate at and propagate from the sub-endometrial myometrium, where receptor density is higher. This demonstrates that contractile wave direction can be controlled hormonally.

infographic.key_insight: Ex vivo adenomyosis tissue showed similar basal contractions to controls, but 1.8-fold higher oxytocin receptor density and a smaller oxytocin-induced increase in contraction frequency.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings inform research into altered uterine oxytocin signaling in adenomyosis, without establishing implications for diagnosis or treatment.
method: Prospective ex vivo case-control study of hysterectomy tissue from premenopausal women.
Video-based spatiotemporal mapping measured contractions across the myometrium before and after oxytocin.
Immunofluorescence with machine learning-assisted segmentation quantified oxytocin receptor density.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study enrolled 16 adenomyosis patients and 12 controls; contractility analysis used 57 strips from 11 versus 8 patients, and immunofluorescence included 10 versus 9 patients.
infographic.watch_item: Small, ex vivo hysterectomy cohorts limit generalizability to uterine activity in vivo, and the abstract provides no validation metrics for the machine learning-assisted segmentation.
infographic.paper_title: Spatiotemporal mapping of ex vivo myometrial contractions in adenomyosis

title: Serum Raman spectroscopy as a blood-based triage test for bladder cancer: a retrospective proof-of-concept study
authors: Milligan, K.; Smith, I.; Flugge, A.; Fakhrua Aldeen, N.; Shine, B.; Muldoon, C.
abstract: BackgroundBladder cancer remains one of the most common urological malignancies. Current diagnostic pathways rely heavily on cystoscopy, an invasive investigation with significant cost and resource implications. A rapid blood-based assay capable of improving patient stratification before cystoscopy could reduce unnecessary invasive investigations while maintaining diagnostic sensitivity. MethodsArchived serum samples from patients with histologically confirmed bladder cancer and symptomatic control subjects were analysed using dried-serum Raman spectroscopy. Raman spectra were incorporated into supervised machine-learning classification models to generate predicted probabilities of bladder cancer. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. ResultsThe study included 49 patients with bladder cancer and 97 symptomatic controls. Predicted probabilities of bladder cancer were substantially higher in cancer patients than in controls. The Raman classifier demonstrated excellent diagnostic discrimination (AUC approximately 0.90). Incorporation of age into the classification model produced little additional improvement (AUC approximately 0.91). ConclusionsMachine learning-assisted analysis of dried-serum Raman spectra demonstrates promising diagnostic performance for bladder cancer. Prospective evaluation is warranted to determine its role as a minimally invasive triage test within contemporary bladder cancer diagnostic pathways.

infographic.key_insight: A machine-learning classifier using dried-serum Raman spectra showed promising discrimination between bladder cancer patients and symptomatic controls (AUC approximately 0.90).
infographic.clinical_relevance: If prospectively validated, this blood-based approach could help triage patients before cystoscopy and potentially reduce unnecessary invasive investigations.
method: Analysed archived serum using dried-serum Raman spectroscopy.
Applied supervised machine learning to estimate bladder cancer probabilities.
Evaluated ROC performance and the added value of age.
infographic.evidence_signal: In this retrospective study of 49 bladder cancer patients and 97 symptomatic controls, AUC was approximately 0.90 with Raman spectra and 0.91 after adding age.
infographic.watch_item: This small retrospective proof-of-concept study does not establish whether the test can safely reduce cystoscopies; prospective validation is needed.
infographic.paper_title: Serum Raman spectroscopy as a blood-based triage test for bladder cancer: a retrospective proof-of-concept study

title: Environmental toxic metal exposure and conditional mortality survival among US adults: a prospective cohort study
abstract: BackgroundHeavy metal exposure has been associated with mortality, but differences in early and median survival times remain unclear. We estimated associations of blood lead and mercury and urinary cadmium and arsenic at lower conditional survival-time quantiles. MethodsWe linked the 1999-2014 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey to mortality records through Dec 31, 2019, including 24,338 adults aged 40 years or older. Weighted censored quantile regression estimated associations at the 10th, 25th, and 50th percentiles, adjusting for age and other confounders across five imputations. Mercury and arsenic analyses used 2003-2014 cycles; urinary-metal cohorts required observed estimated glomerular filtration rate [≥]60 mL/min per 1.73 mZ. FindingsOf 24,338 participants, 6,992 died. Doubling urinary cadmium was associated with 1.71-1.92, 1.50-1.67, and 1.35-1.53 years shorter conditional survival at the 10th, 25th, and 50th percentiles (n=7,061). Corresponding blood lead estimates were 0.63-0.71, 0.55-0.65, and 0.61-0.63 years shorter (n=24,021). Some median estimates were not estimable. Cadmium associations persisted after lead adjustment; lead associations did not persist after cadmium adjustment. Arsenic had no statistically significant association with mortality in this study. Mercury was associated with longer survival despite adjustment for fish or omega-3 intake, possibly reflecting residual confounding. InterpretationLow-to-moderate cadmium exposure was associated with shorter survival, with the largest absolute loss among adults who die earliest. These findings support continued efforts to reduce cadmium exposure, with particular benefit for adults most vulnerable to premature death. FundingNone. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed from database inception to Nov 10, 2026, without language restrictions, using metal names and biomarker terms combined with "mortality", "survival", "quantile regression", "life expectancy", and related terms. We prioritised prospective studies in adult populations and systematic reviews, supplemented by targeted searches for analyses of survival time. Previous studies have associated lead and cadmium exposure with higher all-cause and cardiovascular mortality. Evidence for mercury has varied across populations and exposure levels, and findings for low-level arsenic exposure in US adults have been less conclusive. Most cohort studies reported relative hazards, although earlier research examined metal-associated differences in longevity and used machine learning to investigate variation in lead-associated survival. Evidence remained limited on how associations with metal biomarkers differ between early and median conditional survival times in general populations. Added value of this studyAmong 24,338 US adults aged 40 years or older in NHANES 1999-2014, with mortality follow-up through 2019, we estimated associations of four metal biomarkers with the 10th, 25th, and 50th conditional percentiles of survival time after examination. Censored quantile regression provided estimands in years of life. In the urinary cadmium cohort of 7,061 participants with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of at least 60 mL/min per 1.73 mZ, a doubling of cadmium was associated with 1.71-1.92 years shorter to 10% mortality, compared with 1.35-1.53 years at the median. The cadmium associations persisted in NHANES III, although the largest estimate in that cohort was at the median. Lead and survival time associations were attenuated after adjustment for cadmium. Arsenic estimates were not significant. We observed positive association between blood mercury and survival time, which might reflect some residual confounding that we couldnt control for. Implications of all the available evidenceThe evidence supports continued population-level efforts to reduce cadmium and lead exposure. With CQR, we were able to estimate the survival differences in years of life and for earlier deaths, providing valuable information for public health messages. Future studies using repeated exposure measurements and evaluations of exposure-reduction policies are needed.

infographic.key_insight: Doubling urinary cadmium was associated with 1.71–1.92 years shorter survival at the 10th percentile, with smaller differences at later survival percentiles.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The findings support population-level efforts to reduce cadmium exposure but do not establish causality or guide individual prognosis.
method: Linked NHANES 1999–2014 data for US adults aged 40 or older to mortality records through 2019.
Used weighted censored quantile regression at the 10th, 25th, and 50th survival percentiles, adjusting for confounders across five imputations.
Measured blood lead and mercury and urinary cadmium and arsenic; urinary-metal analyses required preserved kidney function.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 24,338 adults, 6,992 died; cadmium associations in 7,061 participants persisted after lead adjustment, whereas lead associations did not persist after cadmium adjustment.
infographic.watch_item: Observational associations may reflect residual confounding, particularly the apparent longer survival associated with mercury.
infographic.paper_title: Environmental toxic metal exposure and conditional mortality survival among US adults: a prospective cohort study

title: A data-driven regional amyloid PET score predicts cognitive decline beyond Centiloid
authors: Hirose, T.; Akamatsu, W.; Kato, T.
abstract: BackgroundThe Centiloid (CL) scale standardizes global amyloid PET quantification and is widely used to define amyloid positivity. As a global summary measure, however, CL may not fully reflect the regional distribution of amyloid deposition, which can carry additional prognostic information about the rate of cognitive decline. ObjectiveTo develop and externally validate a fixed, regional amyloid PET composite score that complements CL for predicting cognitive decline in Alzheimers disease. MethodsThe Regional Amyloid PET Score (RAPS) was derived from 82 FreeSurfer regions using machine learning with bootstrap stability selection to predict the rate of change in CDR-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) in 433 amyloid-positive ADNI participants imaged with [18F]florbetapir (n = 357) or [18F]florbetaben (n = 76). The fixed nine-region weights were applied without retraining in a small ADNI [18F]florbetaben subgroup (N = 71, 68 of whom were in the discovery cohort; sensitivity analysis) and two external validation cohorts, NACC SCAN (N = 1531; four tracers) and OASIS-3 (N = 428). ResultsRAPS comprised nine regions. In ADNI post-selection evaluation, RAPS correlated more strongly with CDR-SB slope than CL and showed higher discrimination of rapid decliners (AUC 0.813 vs 0.708). RAPS remained associated with progression after CL adjustment in both external cohorts, although neither external AUC difference was significant. Cross-cohort meta-analysis including ADNI development and the two external cohorts favored RAPS alone over CL alone (pooled {Delta}AUC +0.069; I2 = 1.6%). ConclusionsRAPS, a fixed regional amyloid PET-derived score, may complement CL for prognostic stratification in Alzheimers disease research.

infographic.key_insight: A fixed nine-region amyloid PET score may add information beyond global Centiloid measures for predicting cognitive decline.
infographic.clinical_relevance: RAPS may complement Centiloid for prognostic stratification in Alzheimer’s disease research, but clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Used machine learning with bootstrap stability selection across 82 brain regions in 433 amyloid-positive ADNI participants.
Derived a fixed nine-region score to predict change in CDR–Sum of Boxes.
Applied weights without retraining in NACC SCAN and OASIS-3 external cohorts.
infographic.evidence_signal: External cohorts totaling 1,959 participants showed progression associations after Centiloid adjustment, but neither external AUC improvement was statistically significant.
infographic.watch_item: The pooled AUC gain included development-cohort results, and the small ADNI sensitivity subgroup largely overlapped with training data.
infographic.paper_title: A data-driven regional amyloid PET score predicts cognitive decline beyond Centiloid
